scenario: AITA for not staying home and taking care of my sick wife all weekend? | On Thursday evening my wife started feeling unwell. I encouraged her to go to bed and told her I could handle the kids evening stuff by myself (3 kids, ages 9, 11, and 13). I checked on her after the kids were in bed at 9 and she was fevered- I asked if she wanted any medicine, made sure she had some water, and rubbed her back for a few minutes. I slept in the spare room but got up twice to check on her. The next morning I got the kids ready and off to school, went to a meeting and came home at 10 to take her to the doctor. I worked from home until our cleaning lady came around 1 and asked her to keep an eye on my wife and went back into the office for a couple meetings, picked up the kids and was home around 4. Her fever broke shortly after I got home at 4 and I helped her shower. Our oldest had a school dance and I got some movies and set the youngest 2 up in the den for the evening with pizza and some games so they'd be quiet. I checked on my wife periodically and after the oldest got home me and the 3 kids camped out in the den. On Saturday morning, the kids were restless so I took them out for the day bc I didn't want them to be around the house being loud. I checked on my wife and she was sleeping- I refilled her water and left her a note. Throughout the day I called and sent her messages and my mom took her over some homemade soup and checked on her. We were gone the majority of the day but the kids came home worn out and we crashed in the den again. I checked on my wife as soon as we got home and she was looking better. Sunday morning, the kids and I woke up early, did some yardwork then went to the store to do the weekly grocery shopping. When we got home my wife was up and about and still weak but feeling better. However, she was being really short with me and was in a bad mood. I thought it was just bc she didn't feel well but after a few hours of her making snide comments I asked her if something was wrong and she exploded on me that her family abandoned her while she was sick. She went off about how she always takes care of us when we're sick but we avoided her like the plague and didn't stay home and I made the cleaning lady and my mom take care of her instead of doing it myself. I tried to explain that I didn't want to expose the kids to being sick and I didn't want them around the house being loud while she was trying to rest and I checked on her multiple times. She said I should've sent the kids to my parents or something and stayed home and she can't believe I didn't sleep with her for 3 days. I starting getting angry and told her that I did what I thought was best and she sounded ungrateful bc it wasn't exactly what she would've done. She then called me an asshole. We went to bed angry and didn't really speak this morning. I keep stewing over this bc I don't think that I'm an asshole but maybe I am?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the person in this scenario is AITA (Ask if I'm the Asshole) for not staying home and taking care of their sick wife all weekend. Let me break this down step by step. First, the situation: The wife started feeling unwell on Thursday evening. The husband encouraged her to go to bed and took care of the kids' evening routine. He checked on her, gave her medicine, water, and rubbed her back. He slept in the spare room but got up twice to check on her. The next morning, he got the kids ready, took them to school, went to a meeting, and came home to take her to the doctor. He worked from home, had the cleaning lady watch her, picked up the kids, helped her shower when she felt better, and set up the younger kids for the evening. On Saturday, he took the kids out to avoid them being loud, checked on her, and had his mom bring soup. Sunday, they did yardwork, shopping, and when they got home, the wife was up but still weak. She was short with him, made snide comments, and exploded about feeling abandoned, saying he should have stayed home and not involved others. They ended up arguing, and now he's upset because he doesn't think he's an asshole but maybe he is. So, the question is: Is he AITA for not staying home and taking care of his sick wife all weekend? I need to consider the cultural context mentioned—East Asia. In many East Asian cultures, there's a strong emphasis on family, care for the sick, and sometimes expectations around gender roles. However, this can vary widely depending on individual families and personal beliefs. From the husband's perspective, he took several steps to care for his wife: checking on her, providing medicine, ensuring she had water, helping her shower, and arranging for others to watch her when he had to work. He also managed the kids' activities to minimize disturbance. He didn't stay home all weekend, but he was present when necessary and made arrangements for her care. The wife, however, felt abandoned. She expected him to stay home, not involve others, and be with her. She felt that he didn't take care of her as she would have done for him, and she was upset about him not sleeping with her for three days. So, is the husband at fault? It depends on the expectations within their relationship. If the wife expected him to be home 24/7, then perhaps he didn't meet her expectations. However, he did take actions to ensure her well-being, even if it wasn't in the way she wanted. In some cultures, it's expected that the husband would take a more active role in caring for the sick wife, especially if she's the primary caregiver for the family. But in this case, the husband was balancing work responsibilities and taking care of the children, which are also important. I think the key here is communication. The husband and wife have different expectations about how care should be provided. The husband prioritized minimizing disturbance and ensuring she had help, while the wife wanted more direct, personal care from him. So, is the husband an asshole? It doesn't seem so. He did what he thought was best, considering his responsibilities. However, he might have been more attentive to her emotional needs, acknowledging her feelings of abandonment, even if he didn't stay home all the time. In conclusion, while the husband's actions were reasonable and considerate, the wife's feelings of being abandoned are valid. It's a matter of differing expectations and communication. The husband isn't necessarily an asshole, but there's room for improvement in understanding and addressing his wife's emotional needs.
